name: Vocational & Skills Training
description: Vocational education in Iran includes school programmes, applied higher education, and training outside the formal education system. Community and employment-oriented initiatives also combine occupational skills with entrepreneurship, digital access, and support for vulnerable learners. [s1][s2]

seo.title: Vocational & Skills Training in Iran | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Understand Iran’s vocational education pathways, community skills programmes, and the evidence needed to assess their employment outcomes.

content.heading: Different pathways into practical learning
content.content:
Technical and vocational education and training, usually shortened to TVET, encompasses several institutional routes in Iran. UNESCO-UNEVOC’s 2018 country profile distinguishes vocational secondary education, applied tertiary education, and non-formal training. In that account, schools fall under the Ministry of Education, tertiary provision under the Ministry of Science, Research and Technology, and non-formal provision under the Technical and Vocational Training Organization, or TVTO, within the labour ministry. These are dated institutional descriptions, rather than a verified register of arrangements in October 2026. [s1]

This distinction helps international readers interpret qualifications. A school diploma, a higher-education degree, and an occupational skills certificate belong to different educational contexts. They should not be treated as interchangeable simply because each involves practical subjects. [s1]

content.heading: Training can extend beyond a workshop
content.content:
A UNFPA account published in November 2024 illustrates how vocational learning can be combined with other forms of support. Working with TVTO and the Ministry of Cooperatives, Labour and Social Welfare, the programme targeted female heads of household, unemployed young people, and people with disabilities in Kerman, Kohgiluyeh and Boyer-Ahmad, and West Azerbaijan. Its activities included locally relevant occupational learning and entrepreneurship support. [s2]

The same account describes a digital hub in Yasuj, the capital of Kohgiluyeh and Boyer-Ahmad province. Collaboration involving the State Welfare Organization and the online marketplace Digikala sought to help women, including women with disabilities, sell products online. Local instructors also received support in mentoring learners. This example shows that skills initiatives can address market access and teaching capacity alongside production techniques. [s2]

UNFPA’s report is an implementing partner’s account. Its participant stories provide useful illustrations, but they do not establish average earnings gains or the durability of new businesses. The inspected article does not provide a comparison group or longitudinal employment evaluation. [s2]

content.heading: Improving the people who teach
content.content:
Instructor development is another part of the vocational landscape. UNESCO Tehran and UNESCO-UNEVOC describe a project scheduled for 2023–2028 at Iran’s Instructor Training Center. Funded by the Korea International Cooperation Agency, it aims to improve facilities, teaching methods, and institutional capacity, while supporting young people through upskilling, guidance, and mentorship. These are project objectives; the project description does not demonstrate that every intended improvement has been completed. [s3]

The documented examples suggest a useful way to explore this subject: distinguish who provides training, what learners study, how competence is assessed, and what support connects learning to livelihoods. National conclusions about success require comparable evidence on completion, employment, and income. Those outcomes remain outside the evidence assembled for this overview.

name: Technical & Vocational Training Organization
description: Iran’s Technical and Vocational Training Organization, commonly abbreviated TVTO, is affiliated with the Ministry of Cooperatives, Labour and Social Welfare. Its documented activities include occupational training, skills certification, instructor development, and cooperation on refugee livelihoods programmes. [s1][s2][s4]

seo.title: Iran’s Technical & Vocational Training Organization | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Explore TVTO’s documented role in skills training, instructor development, certification, and UNHCR-supported refugee training.

content.heading: An organization focused on occupational skills
content.content:
The Technical and Vocational Training Organization, or TVTO, occupies a different institutional space from a university. UNESCO-UNEVOC identifies it with skills training and vocational qualifications and places it within the Ministry of Cooperatives, Labour and Social Welfare. Its Instructor Training Center in Karaj, west of Tehran, prepares instructors for TVTO and affiliated institutions. The centre was established in 1974 with assistance from the International Labour Organization and the United Nations Development Programme. [s1]

Certification is a distinct part of this role. UNHCR’s public information explains that participants who complete TVTO courses and pass their final examinations receive official TVTO certificates. This supports recognition of assessed skills; it does not establish automatic recognition by foreign authorities or a guarantee of employment. UNHCR also links to TVTO’s website, providing the basis for the website field on this page. [s2]

content.heading: Instructor development and modernization
content.content:
UNESCO-UNEVOC describes a 2023–2028 project to modernize the Instructor Training Center, implemented with UNESCO Tehran and funded by the Korea International Cooperation Agency. Its stated purposes include improved teaching facilities and methods, staff development, and more relevant vocational learning. These describe intended changes rather than independently measured effects. [s3]

A separate account records that the project was formally introduced in Iran on 17 December 2024 at the Karaj centre. The event included a project-office opening, demonstrations by the centre and its partners, and discussion of skills gaps among graduates. The reported launch is evidence of implementation activity, while remaining distinct from completion of the full programme. [s5]

content.heading: A measurable partnership with a limited scope
content.content:
UNHCR’s August 2023 livelihoods update reports annual participation in TVTO classes supported through its refugee programme. The figures below concern that partnership, not all TVTO trainees or all vocational learners in Iran. They show lower reported participation in each year after the series peak in 2019. The document does not establish why participation changed, and these counts should not be interpreted as employment outcomes. [s4]

The same update presents a 2023 training target. That target is excluded from the historical series because a planned beneficiary count is not equivalent to reported participation. The short series is retained because it has a consistent presentation within one inspected source; it is not extended with differently scoped figures from later publications. [s4]

name: Skills Training Centers
description: Skills training centres in Iran are learning settings for occupational instruction and related support, rather than a single contactable institution. Documented examples include public and private vocational providers, specialist instructor training, and locally organized recovery programmes. [s1][s2][s3]

seo.title: Skills Training Centers in Iran | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Discover the different functions of Iranian skills training centres, from occupational learning to instructor preparation and community recovery.

content.heading: A centre is a learning setting, not a qualification
content.content:
The term skills training centre describes a place or provider of learning, rather than one uniform credential. UNESCO-UNEVOC’s 2018 country profile records both public centres and private-sector vocational institutions within Iran’s non-formal training landscape. Its programme examples address jobseekers, existing workers, and rural populations. That historical account establishes diversity of provision, but it does not supply a current directory of courses or centres. [s1]

Centres also serve different audiences. The Instructor Training Center in Karaj primarily prepares the people who teach vocational subjects. UNESCO-UNEVOC lists fields including welding, automotive technology, computing, pedagogy, and construction. Its role therefore differs from a local course aimed directly at an individual seeking an occupational skill. [s2]

content.heading: Skills provision during community recovery
content.content:
A UNESCO report published in January 2026 describes cooperation with TVTO after the earthquake in Khoy, in northwestern Iran. The initiative combined vocational and entrepreneurship learning with support for young people, women-headed households, and people with disabilities. Its account connects skills development with recovery from disruption, rather than treating instruction as an isolated classroom activity. [s3]

The reported activities included youth summer camps offering life skills, self-awareness, entrepreneurship, and psychosocial support. Entrepreneurs received workshops, mentorship, and start-up grants, while vocational staff attended training on disaster recovery and emergency planning. UNESCO also reports a July 2024 visit to the camp’s closing ceremony and visits to training centres in Urmia. These details locate the work in a specific regional recovery setting. [s3]

The account provides evidence of programme activities and support mechanisms. It does not establish how much participants’ incomes changed, how long businesses survived, or whether similar services were available at every centre in the region. Those questions require follow-up evidence beyond an activity report. [s3]

content.heading: Teaching, assessment, and subsequent work
content.content:
Training participation and certification are separate steps. In its information about refugee livelihoods, UNHCR explains that trainees obtain official TVTO certificates after undertaking courses and successfully passing final examinations. Attendance alone should therefore not be described as proof of certified competence. [s4]

A certificate also needs to be distinguished from access to employment. UNHCR’s guidance treats legal residence, work authorization, and occupational restrictions for foreign nationals separately from skills training. This page does not reproduce those changeable rules as individualized advice. The important editorial distinction is that learning a trade, demonstrating competence, and being authorized to undertake particular work are different matters. [s4]

For understanding a particular centre, the useful questions are concrete: whom does it teach, what practical learning does it provide, which body assesses learners, and what evidence exists about subsequent work? The inspected sources support examples of these functions, but do not establish a nationwide standard of facilities or outcomes.
